qs.q: During the investigation of a patient with iron deficiency anemia and a history of caustic oesophageal injury, a squamous cell carcinoma is suspected. In which anatomical portion of the oesophagus is this tumour most typically located?
o: Middle third portion of the oesophagus
Distal third portion of the oesophagus
Upper third portion of the oesophagus
qs.e: Oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma is characteristically located in the middle third of the oesophagus, whereas adenocarcinoma is typically found in the distal third.
qs.s: Tumours of the Gastrointestinal Tract: MCQs

qs.q: A 60-year-old man presents with progressive dysphagia and is found to have a squamous cell carcinoma located in the middle third of the oesophagus. To which group of regional lymph nodes does this tumour primarily spread first?
qs.e: Lymphatic drainage from the middle third of the oesophagus primarily goes to mediastinal, paratracheal, and tracheobronchial nodes. Tumours of the lower third drain primarily to gastric and coeliac nodes.

qs.q: A 69-year-old male presents with persistent hoarseness and dysphagia, and a surgical resection specimen shows laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma. What is a key microscopic finding expected in this lesion?
qs.e: Keratin pearls and intercellular bridges are classic microscopic hallmarks of squamous cell carcinoma. Signet ring cells are characteristic of certain adenocarcinomas like Krukenberg tumors.
qs.s: Pathology Practical and Stains Revision Guide: MCQs

qs.q: A 55-year-old smoker presents with a lesion on the ventral tongue. Biopsy confirms an oral squamous cell carcinoma. Why is this a classic anatomic site for this malignancy?
qs.e: The ventral tongue and floor of the mouth are classic sites for HPV-negative oral squamous cell carcinoma because carcinogens pool in the saliva in these areas. Mechanical friction is not the primary reason for carcinogen accumulation here.
qs.s: Bone & Soft Tissue Tumour Pathology: Must-Know Diagnoses — CAT: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old uncircumcised man presents with a solitary, crusted papular lesion on the glans penis that is diagnosed as an invasive keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. Which risk factor is strongly implicated in the development of this malignancy?
qs.e: Human papillomavirus infection, particularly types 16 and 18, is a well-established risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma of the penis alongside poor hygiene and smoking. Cryptorchidism and DHT are related to testicular and prostate pathology, respectively.
qs.s: Male Reproductive Pathology: Core Conditions: MCQs

qs.q: A 68-year-old woman presents with a unifocal, well-differentiated, keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva. According to the distinct pathological pathways of vulvar carcinoma, which of the following is the most likely preceding condition for this patient's tumour?
qs.e: Non-HPV-related vulvar squamous cell carcinomas typically occur in older women, are unifocal and well-differentiated, and arise from reactive epithelial changes such as lichen sclerosus. Conversely, HPV-related carcinomas arise from VIN and involve high-risk types 16 and 18.
qs.s: Female Reproductive Pathology: HPV, Cancer, PCOS & Pregnancy: MCQs

qs.q: A 68-year-old man presents with persistent firm lesions on the floor of his mouth. A mucosal biopsy confirms oral squamous cell carcinoma. When evaluating the tumor histology, what is the relationship between the degree of cellular differentiation and the biologic behavior of the tumor?
o: Keratinizing tumors have a markedly worse prognosis than anaplastic tumors
Poorly differentiated sarcomatoid variants lack local infiltration
Well-differentiated tumors exclusively metastasize to mediastinal nodes
Differentiation does not correlate with biologic behavior
qs.e: Histologically, oral SCC ranges from well-differentiated keratinizing tumours to anaplastic sarcomatoid tumours, but the degree of differentiation does not correlate with biologic behaviour. Tumor grade does not dictate metastatic potential or clinical aggressiveness in this malignancy.

qs.q: Which of the following histologic findings is characteristic of Bowen disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ) of the penis?
o: Papillary architecture showing virtually no atypia
Malignant cells throughout the epidermis without invasion
Infiltration extending deep into the stromal tissue
Well-formed keratin pearls surrounded by neutrophils
qs.e: Bowen disease is an in situ squamous cell carcinoma defined by malignant cells restricted to the epidermis without stromal invasion. Invasive squamous cell carcinoma, by contrast, shows infiltration into the underlying stroma.

es.q: Detail the risk factors and morphological variants of penile squamous cell carcinoma.
es.m:
- **Predominance:** Squamous cell carcinoma accounts for over 95% of penile neoplasms and is more common in developing countries and uncircumcised males over 40.
- **Risk factors:** Key risk factors include poor hygiene, smegma exposure, smoking, and HPV infection, particularly types 16 and 18.
- **Bowen disease:** Represents SCC in situ, presenting as a solitary plaque on the shaft with malignant cells throughout the epidermis and no stromal invasion.
- **Invasive SCC:** Presents as a gray, crusted, papular lesion on the glans or prepuce that develops into an indurated, ulcerated lesion with irregular margins.

es.q: Discuss the risk factors, histological precursors, and variants of penile squamous cell carcinoma.
es.m:
- **Epidemiology and risk factors**: Over 95% of penile neoplasms arise from squamous epithelium, occurring predominantly in uncircumcised males over 40 years with poor hygiene, smegma exposure, smoking history, and HPV infection (especially types 16 and 18).
- **Bowen disease (SCC in situ)**: Appears as a solitary plaque on the shaft of the penis in older uncircumcised males; histology shows malignant cells throughout the epidermis without stromal invasion, progressing to invasive SCC in about 10% of cases.
